newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China's PLA may not be in HK Monday - China source.
newsitem.headline: China's PLA may not be in HK Monday - China source.

text.p: The unarmed advance guard of China's People's Liberation Army (PLA) garrison for Hong Kong might not arrive on Monday as expected but should come soon, a Chinese diplomatic source said on Friday.
"They won't necessarily be arriving on Monday. It's hard to say whether they'll arrive on that day or not," the source said.
Another Chinese official said the troops might not arrive in uniform but in civilian clothes.

Britain and China last week announced an agreement that 40 PLA personnel could be stationed in Hong Kong from April 21 to prepare facilities, logistics and communications for the future garrison which will replace British troops on July 1.
On that day Hong Kong will revert to Chinese sovereignty, ending over 156 years of British colonial rule.
The PLA advance guard will have no defence or security role and their work will not affect the British troops who will garrison Hong Kong until the handover at midnight on June 30.
After the handover Hong Kong is to be virtually autonomous in all respects except on defence matters and foreign affairs.
A British spokesman said it was not surprising that the advance guard might not arrive on Monday, as the British had still no news from the Chinese side about their travel plans.
"They could come any time from Monday," said British spokesman Roger Goodwin.

"When they come, it's almost certain they'll arrive by road," Goodwin said, indicating the PLA would drive in from the Chinese frontier region of Shenzhen, where the elite future garrison has been based for pre-handover training.
Goodwin said it was likely the contingent would be greeted by British garrison commander General Bryan Dutton at Hong Kong's Prince of Wales Barracks.

In marked contrast to political negotiations, the transfer of defence responsibilities, which has involved direct contacts including rugby matches between the two armies, has been one of the smoothest facets of the transition to Chinese rule.
The future Chinese garrison commander, General Liu Zhenwu, and his political commissar, General Xiong Ziren, have won broad public respect during their visits to Hong Kong.
The British garrison has provided woks for cooking Chinese food, as well as Chinese signs and Mandarin-speaking liaison officers to help the PLA contingent settle in when they arrive at the barracks.
